body:
Essential tourism infrastructure

Tourism infrastructure consists of the facilities and services required for visitors to reach, understand and safely experience a destination.

At pilgrimage and heritage destinations, infrastructure must meet visitor needs while protecting the religious, historical and environmental significance of the place.

InfrastructurePurpose
Roads, public transport and pathwaysSafe and convenient access
Drinking water and sanitationPublic health and cleanliness
Accommodation and sheltersRest and protection from weather
Medical and emergency servicesVisitor safety
Visitor information centresOrientation and cultural understanding
Accessible facilitiesParticipation by elderly people and persons with disabilities

Tourism carrying capacity

Tourism carrying capacity is the level of visitor use that a destination can accommodate without unacceptable deterioration of its environment, cultural significance, infrastructure, community welfare or visitor experience.

Carrying capacity is not simply the maximum number of people who can physically occupy a place. A destination may have sufficient physical space but inadequate water supply, sanitation or emergency facilities.

Dimensions of carrying capacity

DimensionPrincipal consideration
PhysicalAvailable space and safe visitor movement
EnvironmentalPressure on water, soil, vegetation and ecosystems
InfrastructuralWater, transport, sanitation and emergency services
Socio-culturalEffects on residents, religious practices and cultural traditions
Visitor experienceCongestion, safety and quality of experience

These dimensions are interrelated. The effective capacity of a destination may be limited by the most restrictive condition.

Carrying capacity may also change with season, weather, infrastructure improvements, conservation requirements and patterns of visitor behaviour. It should therefore be periodically reassessed.

Crowd management at pilgrimage destinations

Large religious gatherings require advance planning and coordination among organisers, local administrations, police, health authorities and disaster-management agencies.

The principal objectives of crowd management are to prevent dangerous overcrowding, maintain orderly visitor movement, provide essential services and enable an effective response to emergencies.

  • Assess expected attendance and local risks before the gathering.
  • Regulate visitor access according to safe capacity.
  • Provide clear directions, public information and trained personnel.
  • Maintain medical assistance, sanitation and drinking-water facilities.
  • Coordinate transport, emergency services and evacuation arrangements.
  • Review visitor conditions and adjust management measures when necessary.

Environmental management

Large visitor populations can generate solid waste, wastewater, traffic pollution and additional demand for water. Religious offerings and untreated sewage may also affect rivers and other water bodies.

In hill destinations such as Girnar and Pavagadh, erosion, littering, disturbance of vegetation and pressure on pathways require attention.

Suitable responses include waste segregation, sewage treatment, regulated vehicle access, protection of sensitive areas, managed disposal of religious offerings and monitoring of environmental conditions.

Increasing transport or accommodation capacity alone does not necessarily make a pilgrimage destination more sustainable. Conservation, water availability, public safety and the interests of local communities must also be considered.

Prelims focus

  • Carrying capacity includes more than physical space.
  • It varies with environmental conditions, facilities and visitor behaviour.
  • Crowd management involves advance planning and institutional coordination.
  • Wastewater treatment and waste management protect sacred environments.
  • Trap: Higher visitor numbers or improved transport do not automatically indicate sustainable tourism.

[References: Ministry of Home Affairs, Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question 1596, answered 5 February 2014, on crowd-management guidance; Ministry of Tourism, Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 3438, answered 16 December 2024; Ministry of Tourism, Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 5853, answered 30 March 2026, on carrying-capacity assessment and Swadesh Darshan 2.0, consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Five simultaneous constraints determine tourism carrying capacity; the most restrictive can limit it, and capacity changes with conditions.
pictures.caption: The different dimensions of tourism carrying capacity.

title: Tourism Infrastructure, Carrying Capacity and Crowd Management

body:
Sustainable and responsible tourism

Sustainable tourism seeks to maintain the long-term economic, environmental and socio-cultural viability of tourism destinations while meeting the needs of visitors and host communities.

Responsible tourism emphasises the practical responsibility of governments, businesses, visitors and communities to reduce harmful impacts and improve the benefits of tourism.

The concepts are closely related. Sustainability describes the long-term objective, while responsible tourism emphasises the conduct required to achieve it.

Three dimensions of sustainable tourism

  • Environmental sustainability: Conserving natural resources, reducing pollution and protecting ecosystems.
  • Economic sustainability: Generating durable employment, viable enterprises and fair economic benefits.
  • Socio-cultural sustainability: Respecting community identity, cultural practices, religious customs and local ways of life.

Tourism and local livelihoods

Tourism creates both direct and indirect employment.

  • Direct employment: Tourist guides, accommodation workers, transport operators, restaurant workers and heritage-site personnel.
  • Indirect employment: Farmers supplying food, artisans producing goods and enterprises supplying materials or services to tourism businesses.

Community-based tourism can strengthen local economic benefits by involving residents in planning and enabling them to operate homestays, guiding services, craft workshops and other enterprises.

The purchase of locally produced goods may support traditional occupations. In Gujarat, tourism associated with Patan and Kutch can provide markets for textile artisans and other craft communities.

Economic leakage and commercialization

Economic leakage occurs when tourism expenditure leaves the local economy, for example through purchases from external suppliers or profits transferred to businesses located outside the destination.

Consequently, increased tourist spending does not necessarily produce proportionate benefits for local residents.

Commercialization may help practitioners earn income and maintain cultural traditions. Excessive commercialization, however, can lead to imitation products, misleading representations and the modification of rituals solely to satisfy tourists.

Principles of responsible heritage tourism

ProblemResponsible response
Damage to historic structuresConservation and regulated visitor access
Limited local economic benefitsLocal procurement and community enterprises
Misrepresentation of cultural traditionsAccurate, community-informed interpretation
Pollution and excessive resource useWaste reduction and resource management
Intrusion into religious practicesRespect for worship and legitimate access restrictions

Conservation and constitutional responsibility

Heritage conservation is not solely the responsibility of tourism authorities. Cultural institutions, monument-management agencies, local governments, communities and citizens also have important roles.

Article 51A(f) of the Constitution of India establishes the fundamental duty of citizens to value and preserve the rich heritage of India's composite culture.

Article 51A(g) establishes the fundamental duty to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to show compassion towards living creatures.

Both duties are relevant to the protection of sacred landscapes and cultural tourism destinations.

Prelims focus

  • Sustainable tourism has environmental, economic and socio-cultural dimensions.
  • Responsible tourism emphasises actions taken by tourism participants.
  • Community participation can improve the distribution of tourism benefits.
  • Economic leakage reduces the income retained within the destination.
  • Article 51A(f) concerns composite cultural heritage; Article 51A(g) concerns the natural environment.
  • Trap: Tourism commercialization is not invariably harmful, but its impacts require management.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 10, Social Science, 2020 reprint, Chapter 7, pp. 53–56; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Crafts Heritage, pp. 9–14; Constitution of India, Article 51A(f) and (g); Ministry of Tourism, Swadesh Darshan 2.0 guidelines and parliamentary reply dated 30 March 2026, consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Environmental, economic and socio-cultural dimensions contribute to sustainable tourism, each with three practical outcomes.
pictures.caption: The three dimensions of sustainable tourism.

title: Responsible Tourism, Local Livelihoods and Heritage Conservation

body:
Institutional responsibilities

Tourism development and promotion in India are primarily undertaken by State Governments and Union Territory Administrations. The Union Ministry of Tourism supports these efforts through policy, promotion, financial assistance and destination-development initiatives.

PRASHAD Scheme

PRASHAD stands for Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual, Heritage Augmentation Drive.

It was introduced during the financial year 2014–15 under the original name PRASAD, or Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual Augmentation Drive. Its launch took place in January 2015. The expanded title subsequently incorporated heritage development.

PRASHAD is a Central Sector Scheme of the Ministry of Tourism. Its principal purpose is the integrated improvement of tourism infrastructure at identified pilgrimage, spiritual and heritage destinations.

Major areas of assistance

  • Visitor amenities and accessibility.
  • Sanitation and cleanliness.
  • Safety and visitor-management facilities.
  • Improvement of the pilgrimage experience.
  • Development compatible with the religious and cultural character of destinations.

PRASHAD is not restricted to religious destinations belonging to one particular faith.

Swadesh Darshan

The Ministry of Tourism launched the original Swadesh Darshan Scheme in 2014–15. It focused on the integrated development of tourism infrastructure across thematic circuits.

Its themes included Buddhist, spiritual, heritage, Krishna, tribal, coastal and other tourism circuits.

Swadesh Darshan 2.0

The scheme was subsequently restructured as Swadesh Darshan 2.0, with greater emphasis on sustainable and responsible tourism at individual destinations.

Its approach emphasises visitor experience, integrated destination planning, local employment, community participation, environmental sustainability and the long-term operation and maintenance of tourism facilities.

InitiativePrincipal focus
PRASHADPilgrimage, spiritual and heritage destination infrastructure
Original Swadesh DarshanIntegrated development of thematic tourism circuits
Swadesh Darshan 2.0Sustainable, responsible and destination-centred tourism development

Application in Gujarat

Dwarka and Somnath have received attention under pilgrimage-tourism development initiatives. The development of pilgrimage facilities at Ambaji has also been included under PRASHAD.

According to the Ministry of Tourism's parliamentary reply dated 2 December 2024, Dholavira and Dwarka had been identified under Swadesh Darshan 2.0. Gujarat had also received projects under Buddhist and heritage circuit themes of the original Swadesh Darshan Scheme.

Identification of a destination for development does not mean that all associated projects have been sanctioned, constructed or completed. These are separate administrative stages.

Gujarat Pavitra Yatradham Vikas Board

The Gujarat Pavitra Yatradham Vikas Board is associated with the development of pilgrimage destinations in Gujarat. It became an independent body in 1999 after an initial period of association with the Tourism Corporation of Gujarat Limited.

Tourism bodies and pilgrimage-development institutions contribute to visitor facilities, while monument-conservation bodies and religious institutions have distinct responsibilities for heritage protection and religious activities.

Prelims focus

  • PRASHAD and Swadesh Darshan are initiatives of the Union Ministry of Tourism.
  • Both originated in the financial year 2014–15.
  • PRASHAD focuses on pilgrimage and spiritual heritage infrastructure.
  • The original Swadesh Darshan focused on thematic circuits.
  • Swadesh Darshan 2.0 follows a sustainable destination-centred approach.
  • Trap: These tourism schemes are distinct from UNESCO heritage inscription programmes.

[References: Ministry of Tourism, PIB releases on Swadesh Darshan and PRASAD dated 22 July 2015 and 12 December 2024; Ministry of Tourism, PRASHAD and Swadesh Darshan 2.0 scheme guidelines; Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 1119, Development of Religious Tourism in Gujarat, answered 2 December 2024; Gujarat Tourism, Religious Sites, consulted 26 November 2026. Gujarat destination identification is stated as reported on 2 December 2024, not as a current project-completion claim.]

body:
Meaning of intangible cultural heritage

Cultural heritage includes the material and non-material inheritances through which communities maintain their historical and cultural identity.

Tangible cultural heritage includes physical objects and places, such as temples, monuments, manuscripts, sculptures and archaeological remains.

Intangible cultural heritage includes living expressions, practices and knowledge that communities recognise as their heritage and pass between generations.

The UNESCO Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, adopted in 2003, recognises that associated objects, instruments and cultural spaces may also form part of a living tradition.

Intangible heritage is continually shaped by the communities that practise it. Its continuation does not require every generation to reproduce a tradition without modification.

The five UNESCO domains

Article 2(2) of the 2003 Convention identifies 5 broad domains through which intangible cultural heritage is expressed.

DomainIllustrative examples
Oral traditions and expressionsFolktales, oral narratives and traditional chanting
Performing artsTraditional music, dance and theatre
Social practices, rituals and festive eventsReligious ceremonies, fairs and festivals
Knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universeTraditional ecological and seasonal knowledge
Traditional craftsmanshipWeaving, embroidery, pottery and metalworking skills

These domains are broad and overlapping rather than mutually exclusive. A festival may involve oral narratives, musical performance, religious ceremonies and traditional crafts at the same time.

Gujarat examples

  • Garba: A living devotional dance and festive tradition associated with Navaratri.
  • Bhavai: A traditional Gujarati theatre form involving performance and oral transmission.
  • Patola weaving: Traditional textile craftsmanship associated particularly with Patan.
  • Kutch embroidery: Craft knowledge connected with different regional and community identities.

These examples illustrate intangible heritage as a concept. Not every living heritage tradition has been separately inscribed on UNESCO's international lists.

Physical objects and living knowledge

A completed Patola textile is a physical cultural object. The skills, knowledge and traditions through which artisans produce it constitute intangible cultural heritage.

Similarly, a temple is tangible heritage, while its inherited religious ceremonies, devotional songs and associated community practices may constitute intangible heritage.

A written or audiovisual record of a folk song documents that tradition. The living heritage consists of the knowledge and practice through which people continue to perform and transmit the song.

Under the 2003 Convention, eligible intangible cultural heritage must be compatible with international human-rights standards, mutual respect and sustainable development. Historical continuity alone does not justify recognition of every inherited practice.

Prelims focus

  • The UNESCO intangible heritage convention was adopted in 2003.
  • Article 2(2) identifies 5 broad domains.
  • Language is recognised as a vehicle of oral traditions and expressions.
  • Traditional craftsmanship primarily concerns inherited skills and knowledge.
  • One cultural element may belong to several domains.
  • Trap: Intangible heritage is not restricted to traditions that have no associated physical objects.

[References: UNESCO, Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2003, Article 2; UNESCO, Intangible Heritage Domains; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Crafts Heritage, pp. 9–14; UNESCO, Garba of Gujarat, inscription file 01962, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Intangible Cultural Heritage and Its Five Domains
